Leon: "That does not make Noctis his answer."

The board flickered. Leon swallowed.

Leon: "He wrote a statement before he died. He said not to make him noble enough that Noctis could admire him. If this board sends his words to Noctis for permission, it is doing exactly what he refused."

His voice cracked on refused. No one moved to repair it.

Leon: "Enter objection. Personal witness. Leon Varek. Beside."

The board hesitated. That was new. Not acceptance. Not rejection. Hesitation.

Old systems hated being addressed by language they had not been built to digest. Mira raised her hand.

Mira: "Additional objection." Rhea turned.

President Valmont: "Mira Castellan recognized."

Mira stepped onto the lowest fountain stair. Her Green Circle showed at her wrist, small and bright and shaking.

Mira: "Record witness. Cael Nox verbally instructed that ugly copies survive better and corrections written before guilt edited them should not be made prettier. Returning his statement to Noctis is an editorial act."

Aira whispered, "Oh, that is good."

Finn wrote so fast his pen skidded. Mira's voice steadied.

Mira: "Enter objection. Green Circle public witness." The board flickered again.

This time, the warning changed.

**CONFLICTING WITNESS CLAIMS DETECTED.**

Cassian exhaled.

Cassian: "There it is."

Aira: "What?"

Cassian: "The system admitting more than one person exists. Historic." Rhea's seal brightened.

President Valmont: "Enter Council clarification. Death does not terminate witness continuity where active coercion, institutional custody dispute, or hostile terminology risk is present."

The board tried to dim. Halden stepped forward.

Halden: "Enter faculty archive note. Pre-patch substrate conflicts with current Aurelis protected record standard. Board has no authority to privilege origin institution over documented final witness preference." Elira stepped beside Leon.

Elira: "Enter named document witness. Elira Vale. Cael Nox wrote, I wanted to live. I chose anyway. Both are true. Any review that treats death as consent to Noctis custody contradicts the statement." The board flashed white.

For one breath, I thought it would break.

Then old writing appeared beneath the modern warning. Not printed. Not projected. Carved in light from inside the stone.

**DEAD WITNESS STILL WITNESS.**

The grammar was ugly. Older than standardization.

More honest than the board had been all morning.

The fountain water began moving again.

Green Circle students copied the line so quickly the courtyard filled with scratching.

Aira stared at it with open hunger.

Aira: "I am in love with terrible grammar."

Cassian: "Do we notify Haru?"

Elira looked at me, and despite everything, her mouth trembled toward a smile.

The Black Circle settled. Not because the danger had passed.

Because the answer had not needed me alone.

The board accepted the statement.

It did not do so gracefully.

**PERSONAL RECORD ENTERED UNDER WITNESS CONTINUITY.**

Then, after a pause that felt spiteful:

**ORIGIN INSTITUTION REVIEW BYPASSED.**

The courtyard breathed again.

Not all at once. People did not recover like curtains opening. Breath returned unevenly: a sob from the Green steps, a laugh too sharp from Cassian, Leon bending forward with both hands on his knees, Nera covering her mouth, Oric closing his eyes, Rhea lowering her seal before her hand could shake publicly.

Elira leaned against me for half a second. Only half. Enough.

Then a relay bell rang from the council arch. Rhea's expression closed.

President Valmont: "Noctis response."

Aira: "Already?"

Rhea looked toward the accepted record.

President Valmont: "They were waiting for the board to refuse." The bell rang again.

This time, the fountain displayed the incoming seal.

Noctis Dominion College. Formal black. Silver edge.

Lucien's voice did not come through first. That made me colder.

Instead, an older woman appeared in the relay projection. Her hair was iron gray, pinned so tightly it seemed less styled than disciplined. Her uniform bore Noctis rank marks I did not recognize, but Nera went still enough that recognition passed through the corridor behind us like a draft. Nera whispered:

Nera: "Director Vaust." Rhea heard.

President Valmont: "Identify for record." Nera swallowed.

Nera: "Deputy Director of Corrective Continuity. She trained Lucien." Cassian's smile vanished.

Director Vaust looked over the courtyard projection as if counting weaknesses by posture.

Director Vaust: "Aurelis has entered a deceased Noctis student's private document without origin review."

Rhea answered before anyone else could.

President Valmont: "Aurelis has entered a deceased Protected Witness's personal statement under witness continuity."

Director Vaust: "You are relying on a disputed category."

Rhea: "We are relying on a recorded choice."

Director Vaust's gaze moved to Leon.

Director Vaust: "Leon Varek." Leon straightened.

Director Vaust: "Your family will be disappointed to see you lend your name to a procedural disturbance." Leon went very still.

There it was. Not a blade. A hook. Family, disappointment, reputation, the old vocabulary of making obedience sound like love. Leon opened his mouth. Nothing came out. Elira started to move.

He lifted one hand slightly. Stop. She stopped.

Leon looked at Director Vaust.

Leon: "My family has survived worse than my first correct sentence."

Aira made a wounded sound of admiration.

Director Vaust did not blink.

Director Vaust: "Cleverness is not standing." Mira stepped forward.

Mira: "Neither is ownership."

The whole courtyard seemed to realize at once that a Green Circle student had interrupted a Noctis director in public.

Director Vaust's gaze moved to her.

It was not dramatic. She did not sneer. She did not threaten. She simply looked, and every habit Aurelis had taught Green students about making themselves smaller tried to drag Mira backward by the bones. Finn moved beside her. Then another Green student.

Then two more. No one stood in front.

Mira's hands shook. Her voice did not.

Mira: "Cael Nox's statement names the risk of Noctis admiration. Your objection confirms relevance."

Director Vaust: "And you are?" Mira lifted her notebook.

Mira: "Still copying."

For one second, Cassian looked like he might propose marriage to the sentence as a concept. Director Vaust's eyes cooled.

Director Vaust: "Aurelis has allowed public witnesses to mistake emotional participation for legal competence."

Halden answered, and his voice had the precise flatness of a man discovering someone had insulted his favorite kind of evidence.

Halden: "Public witness is not legal competence. It is evidentiary distribution. You may challenge interpretation. You cannot unmake copies already observed by independent parties."

Director Vaust: "Professor Halden. I expected better rigor from you."

Halden: "Then you expected flattery."

Aira actually stopped breathing for a second.

Rhea's mouth twitched and died before becoming expression.

Director Vaust ignored the insult with professional discipline.

Her gaze moved at last to me.

Director Vaust: "Haru Aerlen." The courtyard changed temperature.

Elira's hand tightened around mine.

Director Vaust: "Do you endorse this misuse of a dead student's name?"

There were many traps in the question.

Endorse turned me into authority. Misuse turned defense into desecration. Dead student's name turned Cael into an object I could either claim or abandon.

Lucien had learned from her. That was obvious now.

I looked at the relay projection and felt every eye in the courtyard arrive at my back.

The Black Circle did not rise. That was my answer before words.

Haru: "No."

Director Vaust's expression did not change, but the courtyard did. Fear moved. Confusion followed. I continued.

Haru: "I do not endorse Cael's statement. It does not need my endorsement." Leon looked at me.

Haru: "I witnessed it being read. I object to Noctis custody. I refuse to become the authority that makes his words valid."

Director Vaust: "Convenient restraint."

Haru: "Difficult restraint."

Elira's thumb moved once across my knuckle.

Haru: "He wanted to live. He chose anyway. Both are true. If Noctis wants to challenge that, challenge the sentence. Do not ask me to stand over it so you can accuse me of casting a shadow."

Director Vaust watched me for a long moment. Then she smiled.

It was not Lucien's smile. Lucien smiled like a blade pretending to be a mirror. Vaust smiled like a locked door that had never needed to pretend.

Director Vaust: "Very well. Noctis challenges the sentence." Nera whispered:

Nera: "No."

Director Vaust: "Cael Nox could not simultaneously want life and choose death under coercive conditions created by Aurelis proximity. The statement is emotionally compelling, legally unstable, and medically suspect. Noctis requests suspension of publication pending spirit-state verification."

Maelin's healer bag hit the stone with a thud.

Maelin: "Absolutely not."

Director Vaust looked at her.

Maelin: "No one is using necromantic adjacent verification language on a dead child because you dislike his handwriting."

The courtyard went silent enough to hear the fountain.

Director Vaust: "Healer..."

Maelin: "Senior Restoration Healer Maelin Orr. Medical objection. Ethical objection. Human objection, if your office still accepts those in any format." Cassian whispered:

Cassian: "I am definitely notifying Haru."

I did not look away from Vaust. Rhea stepped forward.

President Valmont: "Aurelis rejects spirit-state verification. Cael Nox's death was witnessed, recorded, and ritually completed. Noctis will not reopen his death as a route to overwrite his life."

Director Vaust: "Then Noctis files formal complaint."

President Valmont: "Accepted."

Director Vaust: "And requests immediate sequestration of all copies."

Mira, Finn, Aira, and half the courtyard said, "No," at the same time. It was not elegant. It was magnificent. Rhea did not smile.

President Valmont: "Denied."

Director Vaust's projection dimmed at the edges.

Before it vanished, she looked at me one last time.

Director Vaust: "Power surrounded by mourners is still power, Haru Aerlen."

Haru: "Yes." My breath steadied against the cold air.

That answer surprised her more than denial would have.

Haru: "That is why they are allowed to say no."

The projection ended. No dramatic crack. No explosion. No immediate attack.

Only the accepted statement on the board, the old line beneath it, and the sound of too many students breathing like people who had just learned procedure could be survived if enough hands refused to let go of the page.

Then Leon sat down on the fountain step. Hard.

Cassian moved first, which he disguised as impatience.

Cassian: "Elegant collapse. Very Blue Circle. Excellent posture until the end." Leon covered his face.

Leon: "Shut up." Cassian sat beside him.

Cassian: "Beside shut up or distant shut up?" Leon laughed. It came out broken.

Cassian looked at the board and stopped joking.

For several minutes, no one asked the courtyard to move on.

That became its own kind of ceremony.

Students approached the board one at a time. Not to bow. Not to worship. To copy. Some wrote the full statement. Some wrote only one line. Some copied the old grammar: Dead witness still witness. A Yellow Circle student hesitated before the Green steps, then asked Finn if he had spare paper. Finn gave him the lunch receipt copy without thinking. The Yellow student stared at it, then accepted it like a relic with grease stains.

Nera stood at the edge of the fountain, reading Cael's sentence again and again. Oric remained beside her.

Darian watched them both with the look of someone realizing defection did not end when one left an institution. It continued each time one refused to carry the institution's habits into a safer room.

Elira leaned more heavily against me. Maelin noticed instantly.

Maelin: "Vale."

Elira: "I know."

Maelin: "Your knowing has historically poor compliance."

Elira closed her eyes for half a breath.

Elira: "Two minutes."

Maelin: "One."

Elira: "Ninety seconds."

Maelin: "Because grief apparently negotiates." I almost smiled. Then Elira whispered:

Elira: "I hate that he had to write it." The almost-smile disappeared.

Haru: "Yes." I met their gaze without looking away.

Elira: "I hate that it is good."

I understood that too. Sometimes a true sentence was beautiful because harm had cornered someone into making it exact. Admiring it felt too close to accepting the corner.

Haru: "Then we do not call it beautiful." She opened her eyes.

Haru: "We call it kept."

Elira looked at the board.

Elira: "Kept."

Maelin gave us the ninety seconds and pretended it was because she needed to repack her bag.

At the end of them, Aira approached with three copies in her hands.

Aira: "Formal, handwritten, ugly."

Elira: "Those are the categories?"

Aira: "They are now."

She gave the formal copy to Rhea, the handwritten one to Mira, and the ugly copy to Leon.

Leon looked at the blotched page.

Leon: "Why me?"

Aira: "Because if I give you the neat one, you will try to become worthy of it, and I am too tired to watch that." Leon stared at her.

Then he folded the ugly copy with more care than he had used for any academy assignment in his life.

Leon: "Fine." Cassian leaned over.

Cassian: "Frame it badly."

Leon: "I will burn you."

Cassian: "There he is."

The courtyard loosened around them. Not healed. Loosened. There was a difference, and for once the difference did not feel like failure.

Rhea sealed the public board at noon. Not closed. Sealed.

The statement remained visible behind protective glass-light. Around it, copies continued to multiply through hands the institution had once trained itself to ignore. Green Circle students made the first ring. Blue students joined next. A few Red. Yellow last, as usual, but not never.

By early afternoon, Dead witness still witness had appeared in six margins, three formal objections, one badly drawn poster, and a chalk line on the lower fountain stone that Dren walked past twice without ordering removed.

The phrase was not doctrine. Elira had been right. Doctrine was too clean.

It was practice. Practice could be repeated. Practice could be corrected. Practice could survive ugly.

That evening, after Maelin forced Elira back to the witness cottage and Rhea disappeared into what Aira called the paperwork furnace, I returned to Cael's room alone. Not entirely alone.

No one let me do that anymore, and they were right.

Cassian stood in the corridor with his back to the wall, pretending to inspect a ceiling crack. He had two knives hidden on him and one pastry openly in hand. Leon sat three doors down with the slate stone in his palm, staring at nothing. Aira occupied the hall bench with a notebook and the posture of a person who would claim she happened to be there if anyone asked.

Elira had wanted to come.

Maelin had said no in a tone that made ancient magic reconsider its priorities.

So I entered without her.

The room looked smaller in evening light.

Maybe it was. Rooms changed after records entered them. Some became shrines. Some became evidence. Some became traps. I did not want Cael's room to become any of those things if I could help it.

I stood by the desk and looked at the empty space where the letter had been.

Power offered me several impossible kindnesses.

It could remember the pressure of his hand on the paper. It could draw a shadow of the last minute he spent here. It could ask the old room what it had witnessed and force the walls to answer in images bright enough to hurt. The Black Circle knew ways to make absence speak. That was the problem.

Absence was allowed to be silent.

I placed my hand flat on the desk.

Haru: "Thank you." No magic answered. Good.

The drawer handle caught my eye.

I remembered the list. Not instructions. Names. Questions.

I did not open it. Mira had copied it. Rhea had sealed it. Leon had seen it. The original remained here because removing every trace from a dead student's room felt too much like cleaning the room for the next use.

Instead, I sat in the chair.

Not the companion chair from the annex. This one was plainer, narrower, and badly balanced. It creaked under me like protest.

For several breaths, I let myself imagine the life Cael had not had time to mistrust. Breakfast without evaluation.

Classes where wrong answers did not become discipline.

Leon asking terrible questions and learning better ones.

Aira forcing him to annotate his own sarcasm for public record.

Elira teaching him that no could be gentle without becoming weak.

Me learning whether he preferred tea or coffee or neither because Noctis had probably ruined both by attaching them to schedules. Small things.

The Black Circle stirred with grief sharp enough to become weather. I closed my eyes.

Haru: "No."

The word was not for Cael.

It was for me. No restoration. No echo.

No bending the room until loss became something easier to look at.

Elira had died in my arms and come back because death had been forced through a hostile route still attached to life. Cael had chosen in a field of consequences none of us could make clean. Those were not the same. If I blurred them because grief wanted one more miracle, I would make every future death a referendum on whether I had loved hard enough to break the world.

That way lay worship. And hatred. And madness wearing mercy. I opened my eyes.

The room remained ordinary. Cruelly ordinary.

Cassian spoke from the doorway.

Cassian: "You still in there?"

Haru: "Yes." The cold pulse behind my ribs remained quiet.

Cassian: "Existentially or medically?"

Haru: "Both."

He stepped in without crossing fully past the threshold.

Cassian: "Good. Maelin requested clarification before threatening me."

Haru: "How considerate."

He looked at the desk, the bed, the folded uniform.

His face changed in the way Cassian's face changed when joking had reached the edge of usefulness and politely stepped back.

Cassian: "I did not know him well enough."

There were many comforting lies available. I chose none.

Haru: "No." Cassian nodded.

Cassian: "Still angry."

Haru: "Yes." I kept my hands resting flat and open.

Cassian: "Good."

I looked at him. Cassian shrugged.

Cassian: "Not because anger is noble. It is not. Mostly it is loud and bad at furniture. But if we skip it, Noctis gets to decide his death was meaningful enough that we are not allowed to be furious."

The chair creaked as I leaned back.

Haru: "Aira would make you write that down."

Cassian: "Aira would improve the grammar and ruin my mystique."

From the hall, Aira called:

Aira: "Your mystique has three spelling errors." Cassian closed his eyes.

Cassian: "See?"

For the first time in Cael's room, I laughed. It was small. It was not clean.

It did not betray him. That mattered.

When I left the room, Leon was still sitting three doors down with the stone in his palm. He looked up.

Leon: "Did you..." He did not finish.

Did you see him? Did you feel anything? Did the room say goodbye? Did being Black Circle make death less final for you than for the rest of us?

I sat beside him on the floor.

Cassian remained by the door. Aira's pencil stilled.

Haru: "No."

Leon looked at the stone.

Leon: "Good."

That was not the answer I expected. Leon swallowed.

Leon: "I thought I wanted something. A sign. A message. Anything. Then the board tried to send his words back to Noctis, and I realized... I do not want more of him taken for answers."

The stone sat in his palm, dull and gray and doing no magic at all.

Leon: "I can keep this without making it speak."

Haru: "Yes." My breath steadied against the cold air. Leon nodded. His shoulders shook once.

He did not apologize. That was also practice.

Later, Elira read the ugly copy in bed with a blanket around her shoulders and Maelin stationed outside the cottage door like a medical curse. I sat beside her, close enough for warmth, far enough that the page belonged to her hands. The lamp was low.

The cottage smelled faintly of cedar smoke and bitter tonic.

Elira read the sentence three times.

I wanted to live. I chose anyway. Both are true.

On the third reading, tears slipped down her face.

Elira: "I wish he had written something worse."

Haru: "Worse?"

Elira: "Messier. Petty. Unfair. Something that would make me angry at him instead of at everything."

Her hand tightened around the page.

Elira: "He was allowed to be unfair."

I thought of Cael's controlled handwriting, trained almost to damage. Even his final refusal had tried not to take up too much room.

Haru: "Then we can be unfair for him sometimes." Elira looked at me.

Haru: "Not in the record. In the room."

She folded forward until her forehead touched my shoulder.

Elira: "I am furious that he saved me." There it was.

The sentence beneath all the careful ones.

I put my hand near her back and waited until she leaned into it before touching.

Haru: "I know."

Elira: "I am grateful."

Haru: "I know."

Elira: "I hate being grateful."

Haru: "I know."

The Black Circle did not move. It had no answer for guilt that would not become violence if mishandled.

Elira cried quietly, which was worse than sobbing because quiet grief kept trying to be considerate.

When she could speak again, she said:

Elira: "Do not let me make his death into a debt."

Haru: "I won't." Elira lifted her head.

Elira: "And do not make that your debt either." I almost looked away.

She caught my face between both hands before I could.

Her palms were warm. Still too thin from recovery. Still alive.

Elira: "Haru."

Haru: "I hear you."

Elira: "No. Answer."

The seven lines in her pendant glowed faintly. Not command. Witness. I breathed.

Haru: "I will try not to make his death into my debt."

Elira: "Try honestly?"

Haru: "Try honestly."

She studied me, found the answer imperfect, and accepted it because perfect answers had done enough damage.

Elira: "Good."

Outside, the academy bell rang evening close.

It sounded better than the morning bell. I disliked that.

Some part of me wanted the world to remain audibly broken until it had earned repair. But bells were not moral instruments. They rang because someone pulled the line, because metal held shape, because sound did not know whom it had failed to mourn.

Elira leaned against me again.

Elira: "Tomorrow, they will ask what the sentence means."

Haru: "Yes." I met their gaze without looking away.

Elira: "What will we say?"

I looked at the ugly copy in her lap.

Haru: "That it means what it says." She closed her eyes.

Elira: "That will annoy everyone."

Haru: "Aira will enjoy it."

Elira laughed softly through the last of her tears.

That laugh did not heal anything.

It kept something from closing.

At midnight, someone tried to erase the board.

The alarm did not ring like an attack. It clicked.

One small, offended sound from the cottage mirror, followed by Aira's voice bursting through the relay before the image had fully formed.

Aira: "Courtyard. Now. Not sprinting if medically banned, but emotionally sprinting is authorized."

Maelin shouted from the hall:

Maelin: "Emotionally sprinting still affects pulse!"

Elira was already sitting up.

Haru: "You are not running."

Elira: "I am not running."

She stood with the careful speed of someone prepared to define running as a legal category and win on a technicality. I helped her into her outer robe because arguing would take longer than moving, and because she let me help after choosing to stand.

By the time we reached the Grand Courtyard, the night had turned silver with ward-light.

The public board still stood. That was the first relief. The second was uglier.

Across Cael's statement, someone had written in black correction script:

**EMOTIONAL CONTAMINATION INVALIDATES FINAL DECLARATION.**

The words crawled over his sentence like frost with manners.

Green Circle students surrounded the board in a half-ring. Not guards exactly. Most were in sleep clothes under academy coats. Finn wore two mismatched shoes. Mira's hair was coming loose from its braid, and ink marked one cheek where she had clearly fallen asleep on a page before the alarm reached her.

Leon stood directly before the board with the slate stone in his fist.

Cassian stood beside him, sword drawn but lowered.

Dren stood behind both of them in instructor black, arms folded, looking less like a teacher than a locked gate that had opinions.

Rhea arrived from the council arch with her seal already active.

President Valmont: "Report." Mira answered.

Mira: "Board surface altered at 00:13. No visible intruder. Correction syntax resembles Noctis administrative challenge but lacks relay seal."

Aira, kneeling by the fountain base, added:

Aira: "Because it is cowardly graffiti wearing a procedural hat."

Halden stood on the other side of the board with three floating lenses rotating around the text.

Halden: "Not graffiti." Aira looked up sharply.

Halden: "Residual substrate command. Someone planted it before the board accepted witness continuity. It activated when courtyard traffic dropped below twelve active observers." Finn stared.

Finn: "It waited until fewer people were watching?"

Halden: "Yes." He adjusted his spectacles, clearing his throat.

Dren's voice cut through the cold.

Dren: "Then we give it watchers."

He turned to the gathered students.

Dren: "No crowding the board. No touching hostile script. No dramatic oaths. Pair by class year. Rotate every twenty minutes. If you fall asleep standing, I will classify you as furniture and assign homework to your friends." Cassian whispered:

Cassian: "Inspirational leadership."

Dren: "Veyr."

Cassian: "Moved."

Elira stepped closer to the hostile script.

Maelin, who had followed us with a blanket and the expression of a thunderstorm with certification, made a warning sound.

Elira stopped at the safe mark.

The correction script brightened when it sensed her.

That made the Black Circle go very still. Not quiet. Still.

There was a difference. Quiet meant resting. Still meant aiming.

Haru: "Elira."

Elira did not look away from the board.

Elira: "It is trying to define grief as contamination." Rhea's seal hardened.

President Valmont: "Yes." Her emergency seal rested flat on the dark wood.

Elira: "Then don't erase it immediately." Leon turned.

Leon: "What?"

Elira's face was pale in the ward-light, but her voice held.

Elira: "If we remove it before people see what it tried to do, Noctis can claim the statement was accepted cleanly and later challenged by emotion. Let the correction indict itself." Mira's eyes widened.

Mira: "Copy hostile layer with timestamp." Aira was already writing.

Aira: "Copying. Hating. Copying more."

Finn looked at the phrase again.

Finn: "Emotional contamination."

He sounded less afraid now. More insulted.

Finn: "That is not even internally consistent."

Halden's head turned with academic interest. Finn flushed but continued.

Finn: "If emotion invalidates final declaration, then Noctis funeral honors are invalid too. They use reverence language in death records all the time. Honored sacrifice. Noble closure. Loyal completion. Those are emotional terms."

Aira pointed at him with her pen.

Aira: "Say that again slower."

Finn did, stammering twice and growing steadier on the third sentence. Mira copied him. Then the Green students copied Mira. The hostile script kept crawling, but now every inch it moved produced more evidence against itself.

Leon stared at the board.

Leon: "It waited until fewer than twelve observers."

Rhea: "That appears to be the trigger."

Leon looked at the half-awake Green students, the faculty, the council seals, Elira wrapped in a blanket and fury, me holding the Black Circle down by refusing to be the first answer.

Leon: "Then twelve is not enough."

He placed the slate stone at the base of the board. Not on the statement. Below it.

Leon: "I volunteer first watch." Cassian sighed.

Cassian: "Obviously I volunteer second, because if you stand here alone you will become tragic and unbearable." Mira lifted her notebook.

Mira: "Green Circle witness group volunteers rotating copy watch." Finn raised his hand.

Finn: "And grammar watch." Dren looked at him.

Finn shrank by one inch, then remembered the board had tried to erase a dead boy and straightened again.

Dren: "Accepted."

Elira leaned into me, exhausted now that the first danger had found structure.

Haru: "You need to sit."

Elira: "I know." This time, she did.

Maelin's relief was so aggressive it became almost hostile.

The hostile script reached Cael's final line.

**I WANTED TO LIVE. I CHOSE ANYWAY. BOTH ARE TRUE.**

It tried to cover the words. The board flashed.

The old grammar underneath woke again.

**DEAD WITNESS STILL WITNESS.**

Then, beneath that, a second older line appeared. Fainter. Damaged. Not modern Aurelis. Not Noctis. Halden went completely silent.

That frightened everyone who knew him. Aira leaned forward.

Aira: "Professor?"

Halden read the line twice before speaking.

Halden: "It says... witness remains where circle fails."

The Black Circle pulsed once beneath my shirt.

The fountain water turned dark at the center. Not black like my Circle. Older than that.

For one breath, the reflection in the fountain did not show the board, the courtyard, or the students. It showed a ring carved into stone beneath Aurelis, broken at four points, with a fifth absence in the middle where no color settled. Mira whispered:

Mira: "Circle Zero." The reflection vanished.

The hostile script collapsed into ash-light. No one spoke.

This time, the silence was not empty.

It was full of the next door.

Rhea recovered first because someone always had to.

President Valmont: "Copy everything."

Every pen in the courtyard moved.

I looked at the place where the reflection had been and felt the Black Circle listening from inside me, not with hunger. With recognition. Elira's fingers found mine.

Elira: "Haru?"

Haru: "I saw it."

Across the courtyard, Halden looked at me like a scholar standing too close to a cliff he had spent his life insisting was only a map error.

Halden: "Tomorrow."

Rhea's eyes did not leave the board.

President Valmont: "No." Halden looked startled.

Rhea: "Morning. After sleep. After medical clearance. After copies leave the courtyard. We do not let old magic or new enemies set our schedule at midnight." Aira, still writing, muttered:

Aira: "I would vote for you, and I hate elections."

The old line faded, but not completely.

At the bottom of the board, below Cael's statement, below the hostile correction record, below the witness seals and ugly copies and slate stone, one phrase remained in pale light.

**WITNESS REMAINS WHERE CIRCLE FAILS.**

Cael had kept a sentence.

The sentence had kept a board.

The board had opened a door none of us were ready to enter.

That, I thought, was how the dead changed the world without being used by it.

## Coda: What Waited In The Drawer

Mira found the list in the top drawer after everyone else left.

She did not open it alone. That was the first victory.

The second was that when she called Rhea back, Rhea did not sigh like procedure had become inconvenience. She returned with Aira, Elira, Leon, Nera, and one blank witness slate. Haru stayed in the corridor because the room felt smaller after the letter, and because sometimes restraint meant not making grief widen to fit him.

The drawer opened without magic.

Inside was a second page, water-marked along one edge.

Only three names were fully legible. Iven.

Lysa, followed by a cramped note: **sweets in boot.**

Leon appeared twice. The first had been crossed through so hard the paper thinned. Beside the second, Cael had written only:

**beside?**

Mira's name carried an ink blot and three unfinished words:

**copies survive if-**

Below it, one question began without a name:

**If Nera says no when nobody-**

At the damaged edge, four letters survived: **Tal-**

Mira did not complete them. No one in the room decided whether they were a name, a place, or the beginning of an instruction.

The last complete sentence had no name.

**If I am gone, do not turn this into instructions.**

Mira read it twice before copying.

Then she wrote beneath it, in her own hand: Recognized. Not instructions.

Leon placed the slate stone on the corner of the copy. Cael's unfinished questions stayed beside Mira's answer, and the blank space after his last line looked like somewhere the living were allowed to continue.

===== EPISODE 30 =====

# Episode 30: **What Iven Copied**

## Iven Sahl

Iven Sahl woke before the bell and kept his eyes closed until the room proved it would not punish him for noticing. Old habit.

It had survived rescue, medical clearance, several nights in the east recovery wing, one formal ruling by the Foundation Council, and Maelin's blunt opinion that fear did not become obedience just because someone had removed the person giving orders. Habits were not soldiers. They did not disband when the war moved elsewhere.

The ceiling above his bed was plain white plaster.

Noctis ceilings had been higher. Darker. Meant to make students feel watched by architecture. Aurelis ceilings were lower in the recovery rooms, and the first morning Iven had hated that because low ceilings felt like traps.

Now he thought they might only be roofs. Hard enough. He opened his eyes.

Morning had entered through the curtains without asking permission. It lay across the foot of his bed in a pale rectangle, touching one folded blanket, one borrowed academy sweater, and the pair of boots someone had repaired while he slept. The left boot had a new lace. The right boot still bore a tiny scorch mark near the heel from the Wounded City. No one had polished it away. Good.

He sat up slowly. Nothing happened. Still information.

Across the room, Oric slept with his face turned into his pillow and one arm hanging off the side of the bed. Nera's cot was empty. She had started taking breakfast in the infirmary common room because Maelin had told her she could leave if the room became too quiet, and Nera had apparently decided to test the offer every morning before anyone could revoke it. On the chair beside Iven's bed, someone had left a small paper packet tied with kitchen string.

He recognized the fold. Not the handwriting. The fold. Boot sweets.

For a while, he looked at them and did not touch.

He had sent sweets to Sera after the extraction, not because sweets fixed anything, and not because he wanted gratitude. He had sent them because there were kinds of loneliness that did not need a speech. They needed proof that someone had remembered the exact small shape of hunger.

He had written, **just so she knows someone remembered**, and then asked Mira to carry the packet because asking directly would have turned remembrance into pressure.

Now a packet sat on his own chair.

There was a note beneath the string.

Iven lifted it with two fingers.

**SERA SAID YOU CAN HAVE TWO. SHE KEPT THREE. THIS IS NOT A TRADE.**

Under that, in smaller writing:

**MIRA WROTE THIS BECAUSE SERA SAID THE WORDS AND THEN LOOKED ANGRY AT THE PENCIL.**

Iven stared at the note until the letters blurred. Then he laughed once.

It came out badly. More breath than sound. Oric stirred and muttered something into the pillow that might have been an insult or a prayer. Iven covered his mouth.

The packet remained where it was. Not a trade. The distinction mattered.

Noctis had taught him that gifts were advance payments. Warmth created debt. Food proved ownership. A blanket meant someone had purchased the right to ask why you were shivering. If you accepted anything, you became easier to move.

Aurelis kept failing to behave correctly.

Iven took one sweet from the packet. Then another. Two.

The number made acceptance smaller, which made it possible.

He placed the rest back on the chair, retied the string badly, and looked at his wrist.

The Green Circle answered in a soft ring beneath his skin. Green.

Foundation, the primers said. Sixty percent. Common.

Necessary maintenance and base function.

He had copied that definition so many times at Noctis that the words still sat in his hand even when he did not want them. Foundation. Maintenance. Base function. The official texts had never written **unimportant**. They had not needed to. Noctis had preferred cruelty with clean margins.

But Mira Castellan was Green Circle.

Finn Castellan was Green Circle.

The first student who copied Mira's courtyard note with an inverted letter had been Green Circle.

The kitchen apprentice who hid extra rolls in folded napkins for transfer students who still flinched at serving trays was Green Circle.

The repair aide who had fixed Iven's boot lace and left the scorch mark alone was Green Circle.

The whole academy seemed to lean on Green Circle hands when the beautiful parts of the world broke.

Maybe the definition had always been wrong.

Or maybe the definition had been honest in a language Noctis did not respect. Foundation. The part that held.

Iven pressed his thumb lightly to the ring until the glow warmed against his skin.

It did not become brighter.

It did not need to.

The morning bell rang badly from the west tower. The cracked note wavered, recovered, and joined the others late.

Oric lifted his head just enough to glare at the window.

Oric: "Bell has structural problems."

Iven: "Halden called it brave."

Oric considered that with the grave hatred of someone still half asleep.

Oric: "Professor Halden should apologize to architecture."

Iven smiled before he could stop himself.

The expression felt unfamiliar on his face. Not wrong. Just newly issued.

He dressed quietly, put Sera's note inside the inner pocket of his borrowed sweater, and left the two remaining sweets where Oric would see them when he woke properly. He did not write a note. Not every kind thing needed instructions.

---

Mira's archive station had moved twice since the ruling.

Mira kept winning arguments with furniture.

The first station, near the infirmary hall, had become too crowded after the Foundation Council posted the decision. Students came to read witness summaries, ask whether their copied statements mattered, and stare at the ugly copies as if imperfection might become contagious if they stood too close, cold stone and the smell of drying ink anchoring the words.

The second station, under the east arcade, had failed because rain blew sideways through the arches and Mira had declared that water damage was not a valid form of public discourse.

The third station occupied a wide table in the old bell tower courtyard, close enough to the public boards to see new postings, far enough that no one could pretend they had joined a witness process by hovering with dramatic concern. Two Green Circle aides sorted paper into stacks. A Blue Circle student sharpened pencils with unnecessary intensity. Aira Solen sat on the table's far end, cross-legged and writing three things at once.

Mira stood at the center of it all with ink on her fingers and tape on her sleeve.

She looked up when Iven approached. Not quickly. Not with surprise.

Like she had left room in the morning for him to arrive and was now using it.

Mira: "Iven."

His name did not sound like assignment when she said it. The open door helped.

Iven: "You said I could ask questions."

Mira: "Yes." Her pencil pressed firmly into the rough paper.

He waited for the condition. None came.

Aira glanced over the top of her page.

Aira: "Careful. She means that literally. I asked one question about filing categories and lost forty-seven minutes to moral infrastructure."

Mira: "You took notes."

Aira: "Under duress."

Mira: "You asked follow-up questions."

Aira: "Under intellectual duress."

Iven almost laughed again. He was beginning to worry it might become a medical symptom.

Mira pulled a chair out with her foot.

Mira: "Sit if you want." If you want.

A small door instead of a hand on his back. Iven sat.

For a moment he only looked at the table. Papers lay everywhere, but not randomly. One stack held formal witness statements with Council seals. Another held ugly copies. Another held correction records where students had copied hostile edits exactly, mistakes included, so Noctis could not later pretend the ugliness had been invented by Aurelis. In the center of the table lay Cael's final copied line under a clear protective sheet.

**I WANTED TO LIVE. I CHOSE ANYWAY. BOTH ARE TRUE.**

The sentence looked different in every copy.

Some letters leaned. Some lines broke early. One student had written **BOTH ARE TRUE** so hard the pencil had torn the paper. Another had misspelled **ANYWAY**, corrected it, and left the correction mark like a scar that did not need healing.

Iven touched the edge of the table, not the papers.

Iven: "Cael wrote your name on his list."

Mira's face changed very little.

Iven trusted that about her. Mira did not make grief large to prove she had received it.

Mira: "Aira told me." Aira's pencil slowed.

Iven: "He wrote, 'Ask Mira how ugly copies work.'"

Mira looked at the protective sheet.

Mira: "Then we should answer him."

She took one blank page and placed it between them. Then she wrote a sentence across the top in clean block letters:

**A RECORD HELD BY ONE HAND CAN BE TAKEN.**

She turned the page toward Iven.

Mira: "Copy it."

Iven's fingers tightened around the pencil.

At Noctis, copying had been a test of obedience. The point was not the sentence. The point was whether your hand could disappear into the hand that wrote before you. Every difference became evidence. Every evidence became correction. Every correction became proof that someone should have corrected you sooner. Mira waited.

She did not say it was easy. The patience helped too. Iven copied the sentence.

His first line came out too close to hers. Careful. Imitative. The pencil moved with old fear, matching the shape of authority because that was what his hand knew how to survive.

Then he reached **HELD** and the L tilted too far right. He stopped.

Mira: "Keep going."

Iven: "It's wrong."

Mira: "Yes." She blew graphite dust from the newly numbered page. He looked at her. She was not smiling.

Mira: "Keep going." So he did.

The second half came out worse because now he knew it was wrong and had to keep writing anyway. The space between **ONE** and **HAND** was too wide. **TAKEN** looked angry. He set the pencil down as if it might accuse him.

Mira took his copy, placed a second blank page beside it, and copied his version exactly until she reached the tilted L.

Then she tilted it farther. On purpose. Iven stared.

Mira finished the line, copied his too-wide space, made her own error in **CAN**, and set the page down.

Mira: "Now mine contains yours, and something mine added."

She slid the page to Aira without looking.

Aira accepted it with the solemnity of a priest receiving contraband and copied Mira's copy. Her handwriting was fast, sharp, and impatient with straight lines. She preserved the tilted L, exaggerated the space, kept Mira's damaged **CAN**, and accidentally dropped the final period.

Aira: "I regret nothing except punctuation."

Mira gave the third copy to the Blue Circle pencil sharpener, whose name Iven thought was Talen. Talen copied all three errors and added one of his own, making **RECORD** look like **REC0RD** because the O closed too hard.

By the fourth page, the sentence had become a small procession. Not ruined. Traveled.

Mira laid the pages in order.

Mira: "A perfect copy can be attacked as forgery. Authority likes perfect copies. They look controlled. They look official. They look as if one hand wrote all of them and many hands only pretended to exist."

She touched the first page.

Mira: "But this is my hand." The second.

Mira: "This is yours." The third.

Mira: "Mine again, carrying yours badly." The fourth.

Aira: "My tragic punctuation era." The fifth.

Mira: "Talen's pressure mark."

Talen, who had been trying very hard to become invisible, turned red.

Mira: "Each difference proves another person touched the sentence. Noctis can dispute the first record. They can claim the original was altered, forged, coerced, or taken from context. They have done all four since breakfast."

Aira: "With impressive lack of creativity."

Mira: "But when a sentence travels through many imperfect hands, revoking it requires revoking each hand separately."

Iven looked at the copies.

Iven: "And they cannot."

Mira: "Not anymore."

The words should have felt triumphant. They did not. They felt heavy.

Not bad heavy. Real heavy. The weight of a table that stayed where someone put it. The weight of a cup with a crooked label. The weight of a boot sweet accepted without becoming a contract.

Iven: "What if the error changes the meaning?"

Mira considered the question like it deserved more than reassurance.

Mira: "Then the new meaning belongs to the person who made it. We can mark difference. We can compare versions. We can preserve the original beside the copies. But we do not erase the hand to protect the sentence."

Iven thought about the primers. Foundation. Maintenance. Base function.

He thought about how many times he had copied those words until they became a smaller cage than the room.

Iven: "Can I copy something else?"

Mira placed a blank page in front of him.

Mira: "Yes." Her pencil pressed firmly into the rough paper.

Not what. Not why. Just yes.

Iven took Sera's note from his pocket.

He did not copy all of it. Some parts belonged to Sera, and some parts belonged to the angry look she had given a pencil. But one line kept resting in his mind as if it had been waiting for a page. He wrote:

**THIS IS NOT A TRADE.**

The T in **THIS** leaned left. He corrected it without erasing. The correction made the letter darker than the others. He almost started over.

Then he remembered Mira's voice. Keep going. He finished the line.

Mira did not touch the page until he pushed it toward her.

Mira: "Do you want it copied?"

The question stopped him. Want. Not should. Not may. Not must.

He looked at the sentence.

It was not elegant. It was not official. It had no seal, no witness number, no place in the Council archive unless someone argued very hard and became annoying enough to win.

But it was a sentence he had needed in his own hand.

Iven: "One copy." Mira nodded.

She copied it beneath his version, preserving the corrected T.

Then she made her own difference. The period at the end became slightly too dark because her pencil paused there. Not a trade. Held by two hands.

Aira looked at the page and said nothing.

Iven knew from the silence that she understood.

---

He met Cael near the recovery corridor because grief had poor timing and the academy had too many corners.

For one impossible breath, Iven's mind forgot the funeral, the board, the letter, the Foundation ruling, the black ash-light that had tried and failed to eat Cael's final words. He saw Cael ahead of him in the corridor with the morning at his shoulder, pale uniform loose over a body still learning how much space it could take, and thought: There.

Then the truth corrected him. Not Cael. Leon.

Leon had stopped outside Cael's old room with one hand on the doorframe. The resemblance was not in his face. It was in the way grief made him stand beside things without entering them. Beside the room. Beside the chair. Beside the life that had ended too soon for apology to become practice.

Iven should have turned back. Instead, Leon looked over.

His eyes fell to the folded page in Iven's hand.

Leon: "Archive?" Iven nodded.

Leon: "Mira still terrifying?"

Iven: "Precisely."

Leon's mouth moved like it wanted to smile but had forgotten the sequence.

The corridor held them awkwardly.

Iven had practiced three things to say to Cael before remembering that Cael was not available for conversations anymore. The words had nowhere to go, so they kept knocking around inside him.

One of them escaped toward Leon instead.

Iven: "The charm found someone." Leon looked at him.

Iven: "Cael's charm."

Leon's face changed. Not much. Enough.

Leon: "He gave it away."

Iven: "I guessed he would."

Leon: "How?"

Iven answered before he could make the sentence impressive.

Iven: "He held it three days before passing it on. Something you hold for three days and then give away is already practice. He was rehearsing generosity."

Leon looked down at his own hands.

For a moment Iven saw the old Blue Circle student who had once treated status like armor because no one had taught him what else hands were for. Then Leon flexed his fingers, slowly, as if checking whether the armor had loosened enough to become skin.

Leon: "Cael had honest hands."

Iven: "Yes." He pulled his sweater closer, eyes on the floor.

Leon: "Noctis tried to make that inconvenient."

Iven: "It failed."

Leon gave a small, broken breath.

Leon: "Good."

They stood there a little longer. The room behind Leon remained half-open. Someone had placed a slate stone on the desk, ordinary and smooth, holding down a copied page. The stone did not know it was important.

Its ignorance made it better at being important.

Leon glanced at Iven's folded page.

Leon: "What did you copy?" Iven opened it. Leon read both lines.

**THIS IS NOT A TRADE.**

**THIS IS NOT A TRADE.**

The second version carried Mira's dark period. Leon swallowed.

Leon: "Useful sentence."

Iven: "I think so."

Leon: "Can I..."

He stopped before the request became too large.

The restraint was new enough that Iven noticed.

Iven held out the page.

Leon took a blank slip from the desk. He copied Iven's sentence from Mira's copy, not from the original. His handwriting was cleaner than both, disciplined by years of expensive instruction, but the final word bent slightly downward. Trade.

Like it had become tired at the end. Leon stared at it.

Leon: "I made it worse."

Iven: "Yes." He pulled his sweater closer, eyes on the floor. Leon looked up.

Iven: "That means it's yours."

Leon gave the page back with the careful expression of someone being trusted with something small enough to survive.

Iven continued down the corridor.

He did not look back until he reached the corner.

Leon had placed his copy under the slate stone beside Cael's. The stone held both.

---

Iven's first ordinary class lasted eleven minutes.

Instructor Mora taught foundational ward repair in a room with wide windows and no restraint marks. She explained every tool before passing it down the rows. Students were permitted to choose copper or chalk. The door remained open.

Iven noticed all of that.

Then she rang a brass bell to begin the exercise.

His body left the room before his mind agreed.

Desk struck knee. Chalk shattered under his shoe. Someone said his name. The corridor arrived around him with his back against stone and both hands protecting the channel points at his throat.

Noctis bells meant stand straight, hands visible, wait for correction.

This bell had meant begin.

His lungs did not care.

Instructor Mora stopped inside the doorway. Not closer.

Instructor Mora: "The hall is available. The class is available. Neither choice changes your attendance mark today." Iven stared at her.

Iven: "That is special treatment."

Instructor Mora: "Yes. Injury often requires it."

No apology. No lie that everyone was being treated identically.

Behind her, twenty students tried not to stare and failed in different directions.

Iven looked at the broken chalk near his boot.

Iven: "If I leave, do I fail?"

Instructor Mora: "No."

Iven: "If I return?"

Instructor Mora: "Also no."

The absence of punishment made the choice harder.

He stayed in the corridor until his hands lowered.

Then he picked up the largest chalk fragment.

He returned because the window was wide, the door remained open, and an unfinished ward on his desk had one broken line he knew how to repair. No one applauded.

Instructor Mora did not ring the bell again.

Iven completed one corner of the ward, left the other three unfinished, and wrote beneath it:

**BELL RESPONSE INTERRUPTED WORK. WORK RESUMED.**

Instructor Mora marked the repaired corner correct.

She marked the unfinished sections tomorrow.

A Blue first-year raised his hand before Iven left.

Blue Student: "Should we stop using the bell?"

The whole class looked at Instructor Mora. She looked at Iven.

Not forcing him to decide school policy. Asking whether he had an immediate condition.

Iven considered the brass bell on her desk.

Removing it forever would make the room quieter. It would also let Noctis keep deciding what the sound meant.

Iven: "Say before you ring it. Not today. Next class, once."

Instructor Mora wrote the condition on the board.

**BELL ANNOUNCED. ONE RING. EXIT REMAINS OPEN.**

The Blue student copied it into his notes.

Iven left the chalk fragment on his desk for tomorrow.

As he reached the corridor, Instructor Mora removed the bell from the center of her desk and placed it near the open door. Not hidden. Not centered.

The Blue student adjusted his seat so Iven would have a clear path outside next class. Another student moved the chalk tray within reach without looking at him for thanks. Small changes. Visible. Reversible.

No one announced the class had become kinder.

Iven trusted the room slightly more because it had changed shape without demanding gratitude for the effort.

That was enough for one morning.

For the first time, tomorrow looked less like a threat than a place his chalk might still be waiting.

---

Lunch in the courtyard had become complicated by freedom.

At Noctis, meals were simple because everything was assigned. Students sat by rank, offense, recovery status, and usefulness. Food arrived in portions designed to prove that someone else had measured your need correctly. Talking too much meant arrogance. Talking too little meant concealment. Dropping a utensil could become a moral failure if the right adult needed an example.

Aurelis did not understand the efficiency of cruelty.

Students sat in changing groups. Some ate on benches. Some sat on low walls. Two Blue Circle girls argued over herb bread while a Red Circle boy balanced three bowls for friends who had not arrived yet. A kitchen aide crossed the courtyard with extra fruit and let people take from the basket without writing names down.

The disorder made Iven nervous.

It also made him hungry.

He took a tray because Maelin had once said, "Eat before your body files a formal complaint," and Iven had no wish to discover what body paperwork felt like. He chose soup, bread, and an apple. Then he stood at the edge of the courtyard and looked for a place that did not require becoming part of a group.

Then he saw the girl.

She was younger than him. Eleven, maybe, or younger if fear had been stealing height. She sat near the north planter with her tray balanced on her knees and her shoulders arranged to make the smallest possible target. Her hair was cut blunt at her chin. Her borrowed Aurelis sweater was too large. One sleeve covered her wrist completely. No one sat beside her.

Not because Aurelis had rejected her. Because Aurelis students, having been lectured by Maelin, Mira, Rhea, and probably furniture by now, had become very cautious about not crowding Noctis transfers. The caution was kind. It was also lonely from a distance.

Iven recognized the posture before he recognized why. Minimum space. Maximum invisibility.

Need hidden so well even hunger had to whisper.

He did not walk to her.

He walked toward a nearby patch of low wall that faced the same direction she did, close enough that she could include him if she wanted, far enough that she did not have to defend the space between them. He sat.

In the direction of beside. Not beside.

The distinction mattered enough that he felt it in his knees. He opened his bread.

The girl did not look at him. Good.

They ate in silence while the courtyard kept being too alive around them. Aira passed with a stack of papers taller than good judgment. Cassian crossed after her carrying another stack and wearing the expression of a man who had agreed to help before learning the papers had opinions about wind. Near the fountain, Halden and President Valmont stood over an old map with the shared frown of adults trying not to let mystery set the schedule before lunch.

The girl watched none of it.

She ate soup in small measured bites.

After several minutes, she spoke without turning her head.

Girl: "You don't have to." Iven swallowed before answering.

Iven: "I know."

She held her spoon very still.

Girl: "Then why are you doing it?"

The question had too many possible answers.

Because no one did it for me soon enough.

Because Mira taught me copies can travel.

Because Sera sent sweets back.

Because Cael held a charm for three days and then gave it away.

Because Foundation might mean something better than they told us.

All of that was too much to place on a girl defending soup.

Iven: "I was going to sit somewhere. This wall was here."

The girl's mouth tightened. Not quite belief. Not quite refusal. They ate.

Wind moved through the courtyard and lifted the corner of a posted copy on the public board. Someone had written Cael's last line in blue pencil this time. The color made it look almost gentle. Beneath it, in three different hands, students had copied the old phrase that had appeared after the hostile Noctis script burned out:

**WITNESS REMAINS WHERE CIRCLE FAILS.**

Iven did not understand Circle Zero.

He was relieved by that.

There were already too many things adults wanted children to understand quickly so the adults could feel less late.

The girl followed his gaze at last.

Girl: "Is that about him?"

Iven: "Cael?"

Girl: "The Black Circle."

Iven looked toward the witness cottage. Haru Aerlen was not visible. That seemed polite of him.

Iven: "Maybe partly."

Girl: "Noctis says he contaminated the ruling."

The words arrived flat, memorized, and tired.

Iven had heard that voice from his own mouth before. A sentence repeated enough times to stop sounding like belief and start sounding like weather.

Iven: "Noctis says many things."

Girl: "Aurelis says many things too."

Iven: "Yes." He pulled his sweater closer, eyes on the floor. She looked at him.

Her eyes were dark and sharp with suspicion that had been required too early.

Girl: "Then how do you know which ones are traps?"

Iven thought of perfect copies.

He thought of Mira's tilted L.

He thought of the corrected T in his own sentence.

Iven: "I don't always." The girl's expression closed.

He kept going before she could file him under useless.

Iven: "But traps usually need you to answer faster than you can think."

She looked down at her soup.

Her sleeve had slipped half an inch. Not enough to show her Circle.

Iven: "You can take longer here."

Girl: "Who said?" Iven almost said Maelin.

Then he imagined Maelin appearing from behind a pillar to threaten someone's pulse and decided against summoning that much authority.

Iven: "People keep proving it."

Girl: "People can stop."

Iven: "Yes." He pulled his sweater closer, eyes on the floor.

The girl's spoon touched the bowl once. Softly.

She waited for correction. None came.

Across the courtyard, the west bell made its cracked little sound because someone had opened the tower door too hard. Several students laughed. The girl flinched at the laughter, then seemed confused when nothing followed it.

Iven broke a piece of bread.

Girl: "What Circle are you?"

He held out his wrist. Green light answered.

He did not make it brighter. The girl stared.

Girl: "Foundation."

Iven: "Yes." He pulled his sweater closer, eyes on the floor.

Girl: "Maintenance rank." There it was.

The old definition, polished clean enough to hide the blade.

Iven looked at his own Green Circle and thought about all the versions of the sentence traveling through imperfect hands. He thought about the repair aide leaving a scorch mark on a boot because not everything damaged needed to be corrected. He thought about the kitchen string around Sera's sweets.

Iven: "That's one reading."

Girl: "There are others?"

He was twelve and had no authority.

The lack of authority felt important.

An official definition would have been too heavy. A perfect answer would have looked like another institution arriving to replace the first.

So he gave her the version he had, incomplete and still warm from being made.

Iven: "Foundation means the part that holds while other things fall."

The girl looked at him.

He wondered if he had said it badly. Probably.

Mira would have marked the sentence more carefully. Aira would have made it sharper. Rhea would have made it public policy by evening and somehow still scared a committee into thanking her.

But the girl did not need a perfect record.

She needed something worth carrying.

Her covered wrist moved. Only slightly.

The sleeve drew back enough for him to see a ring of pale green light, unsteady at the edges, as if even the color had learned to make itself small.

Iven did not look too long.

Iven: "You don't have to show it."

Girl: "I know."

She said it like she was testing whether the words belonged to her. Good.

They ate until both trays were empty.

When Iven stood, the girl tensed.

He picked up his tray.

Iven: "I'm returning this."

Girl: "I can see that."

It was the first thing she had said that sounded almost like annoyance instead of defense.

Iven accepted it as progress with teeth.

He carried his tray to the return table and did not look back until he had placed it down.

The girl was still there.

Her sleeve remained pushed back. Not far. Enough.

---

The fourth copy of Iven's sentence reached the public board by accident.

Aira claimed accident, and because Aira lied with style but documented with frightening precision, people believed her only halfway.

The line appeared below a cluster of copied witness notes near the fountain:

**THIS IS NOT A TRADE.**

The first version had Iven's corrected T.

The second had Mira's dark period.

The third had Leon's tired final word.

The fourth, in Aira's hand, had no punctuation and somehow sounded more dangerous for it.

By midafternoon, someone had copied it onto a scrap and pinned it near the infirmary entrance. By evening, a kitchen aide had written it on the inside of the pantry door where students receiving extra food could see it without anyone announcing the kindness aloud. One of the younger transfer students copied it wrong as **THIS IS NOT A TRIAL**, and Maelin declared the error medically acceptable.

Iven saw that copy after dinner.

He stood in front of it for a long time. Not a trade. Not a trial.

The mistake had changed the meaning.

It had not ruined it.

He found Mira near the archive station, wrapping the day's public copies in brown paper against night damp.

Iven: "Someone wrote it wrong." Mira followed his gaze.

Mira: "Yes." She blew graphite dust from the newly numbered page.

Iven: "It's better that way too."

Mira's hands stilled around the string.

Mira: "Sometimes." He waited. She tied the bundle.

Mira: "Not all errors are freedom. Some are harm. Some are lies. Some are accidents that need correction because people deserve clarity. Ugly copies work because we keep the versions beside each other. We do not pretend difference automatically means truth."

Iven looked at the pantry door again.

Iven: "But this one can stay?"

Mira: "This one can stay."

Aira, from behind a stack of record sleeves, said:

Aira: "I give it three days before someone forms a committee around it."

Mira: "I will sabotage the committee."

Aira: "Excellent. I will take minutes." Iven smiled.

This time the expression knew where to go.

Then a Red Circle third-year tried to make the sentence useful.

She arrived with two friends, a perfect braid, and a donation box polished so brightly it looked like it had never met a poor hand. The box had a paper sign taped to the front:

**GIFTS FOR NOCTIS RECOVERY STUDENTS**

Under that, in smaller, prettier writing:

**THIS IS NOT A TRADE**

Iven saw the line and felt his stomach forget what bread was for.

The third-year smiled at him with practiced gentleness.

Student: "You're Iven, right?"

He could have said no.

That was new information. Names at Noctis had not been optional. Here, for one dangerous second, he understood that lying about himself might be possible. He did not.

Iven: "Yes." He pulled his sweater closer, eyes on the floor.

Student: "I'm Dalia Renn. My family supplies winter linens to three hospitals. We thought the phrase was beautiful." Beautiful.

The word slid over the sentence like varnish.

Mira's hands tightened around the brown paper bundle.

Aira stood behind the archive table, already alert. Her first mistake was thinking alert meant correct.

Aira: "Donation boxes require approval through the student welfare office, public ledger review, and anti-patronage language."

Dalia's smile did not move.

Dalia: "Of course. We want to do this properly." The properly landed wrong.

Iven knew because his shoulders had already risen toward his ears.

Aira heard paperwork and drew a sword made of policy. She was good at that. Too good. In a different room, against a different threat, it would have worked. This threat had ribbons.

Dalia turned the polished box so the copied line faced the courtyard.

Student: "We only wanted to help. Unless help is offensive now."

A few students nearby slowed. There it was.

The trap that did not need Noctis seals because ordinary pride could carry it.

If Iven objected, he became ungrateful. If Mira objected, Green Circle witness work became jealous. If Aira objected harder, Dalia became a generous student punished by procedural suspicion. Aira opened her mouth.

Mira stepped on her foot.

Aira made a tiny sound.

Mira did not look sorry.

Mira: "You copied it wrong." Dalia blinked.

Student: "Pardon?"

Mira pointed at the sign.

Mira: "Your T is too clean." Aira stared at her. Iven did too.

Mira lifted her own copy from the bundle, the one with Iven's corrected T darkened by hesitation.

Mira: "This sentence came from a specific hand. The correction mark matters." Dalia's smile sharpened.

Student: "We can fix the lettering."

Mira: "No."

The word surprised everyone, including Mira.

Color climbed her face. She hated that. It made her look younger, and being younger in public was one of the disadvantages adults pretended not to use. She kept going anyway.

Mira: "You cannot fix it by making the mistake prettier. You have to ask whether he wants that sentence on your box."

Dalia looked at Iven. Finally. Not as symbol. Not as recovery category. As obstacle.

That felt worse, but cleaner.

Dalia: "Do you?"

Every answer in Iven's mouth tried to become strategy.

Noctis would have taught yes, because refusing generosity revealed arrogance.

Aurelis was teaching maybe, because people here liked questions large enough to hide in.

Sera's note had said not a trade because Sera said the words and then looked angry at the pencil.

Iven held that anger for a moment. It helped.

Iven: "No." Dalia's friends shifted.

Dalia's smile vanished for half a second before training found it again.

Student: "Then we will remove the phrase."

Iven looked at the polished box. At the word gifts.

At the empty slit where coins would disappear before anyone had chosen what receiving them meant.

Iven: "And the box."

Dalia: "The box is just for collection."

Iven: "It looks like a mouth."

That was not a good argument.

It was not balanced, legal, fair, or easy to enter into minutes. It was true. Mira's expression changed.

Aira's did too, but hers changed into horror first because she had almost argued Dalia into winning the wrong fight beautifully.

Aira: "Iven is right."

The words came stiffly. Not because she doubted them.

Because being socially wrong in public tasted terrible and she had no prepared category for it.

Aira: "I was answering the office problem. This is not an office problem." Mira, still flushed, muttered:

Mira: "Miracle."

Aira: "Do not enjoy this."

Mira: "I am enjoying it privately."

Aira: "You are doing it with your entire face."

The argument was petty. Small.

Useful in the way ordinary weather was useful after a storm.

Dalia looked from one of them to the other and discovered that the audience had stopped forming around her generosity. Students were watching Iven now. Not kindly. Not cruelly. Waiting. That was its own pressure.

He could feel it trying to make him wise. He refused.

Iven: "If people want to give food, put it on the table. No names. No box. No phrase." Dalia's jaw tightened.

Student: "Then how will people know where it came from?"

Mira's answer came too fast.

Mira: "They won't." Dalia looked genuinely offended.

For some reason, that was the thing that made Iven less afraid.

Her generosity had wanted a witness.

His hunger did not owe it one.

Dalia took the sign off the box. Too sharply. The tape tore.

Aira winced at the paper damage and then clearly decided not to have that reaction where anyone could respect it.

Dalia left with her friends and her polished box.

By lunch, a plain tray appeared near the pantry door with bread, oranges, wrapped sweets, and one folded note in kitchen handwriting:

**TAKE IF USEFUL. LEAVE IF NOT.**

No one signed it.

Mira copied the note because she could not help herself.

Then she wrote, very small at the bottom of her copy:

**Better than Dalia's box.**

Iven saw it.

Mira saw him seeing it.

Mira: "That line is not for public archive."

Iven: "It's petty."

Mira: "Yes." Her pencil pressed firmly into the rough paper.

He waited for her to apologize. She did not.

Mira: "Some records are mine before they are useful."

Iven thought about his corrected T.

About Cael's line under the slate stone.

About a girl at the north planter keeping her sleeve half-pushed back because no one had demanded the whole wrist.

Iven: "Good."

The plain tray lasted exactly one hour before someone tried to organize it.

This time it was not Dalia.

It was a Green Circle boy with ink on both cuffs and the desperate expression of a person who had mistaken usefulness for safety. His name was Pellar, Iven thought. Or Pellin. Something with a P that he had heard during public copy sorting and failed to keep because too many new names had arrived without warnings attached.

Pellar brought three columns drawn on scrap paper.

**FOOD LEFT**

**FOOD TAKEN**

**BALANCE**

He looked proud. He also looked terrified.

Mira saw the columns and made a small noise of pain.

Pellar: "It's not a ledger. Not officially. I just thought if people knew supply levels, they could replace things before the tray went empty."

Aira, still recovering from being wrong about Dalia's box, visibly forced herself not to answer first.

The effort looked almost medical.

Mira: "Why balance?"

Pellar tapped the third column.

Pellar: "So nobody takes too much." The words were ordinary.

They were also a door with old hinges.

The younger transfer girl from the north planter had come near the pantry table for an orange. She stopped with her hand halfway out. Sleeve still pushed back enough to show Green. Her fingers closed on air, then retreated to her side. Iven saw it.

Pellar did too, and his face changed with horror.

Pellar: "I didn't mean--"

The apology rushed out too fast.

Fast apologies were sometimes another way to ask the injured person to make the room kind again. The girl stepped back.

Iven moved before he knew what he was doing. Not toward her. Toward the paper. He picked it up.

Pellar flinched as if expecting punishment.

Iven held the three-column sheet and felt the old Noctis part of his hand understand it perfectly. Food left. Food taken. Balance. Proof that hunger had been measured. Proof that receiving could become debt without anyone using the word.

The paper was not evil. That was inconvenient.

Pellar had not built a trap. He had built a nervous little bridge and accidentally made it look like a gate.

Iven: "Supply is useful." Pellar blinked.

Iven tore off the third column. Not neatly.

The rip ran through the word balance until only **bal** remained on one side and **ance** on the other. Aira made a strangled sound because she was apparently capable of mourning paper while respecting trauma.

Iven gave the torn balance column back to Pellar.

Iven: "This part is not." Pellar stared at it. Then at the girl.

Pellar: "I'm sorry."

This time he said it slower. Not asking her to fix his face.

The girl looked at the tray.

At the oranges. At Iven.

Girl: "Can there be a sign?" Mira's pencil lifted.

The girl noticed and frowned.

Girl: "Don't write me down."

Mira lowered the pencil immediately.

Mira: "Sorry."

That apology was quick, but not demanding. It landed and stayed small.

The girl thought for a moment.

Girl: "A sign that says you can take one and also more than one." Pellar looked confused.

Girl: "Because one sounds safe until you're still hungry." Iven's chest hurt.

He did not make it visible if he could help it.

Aira reached for a blank scrap, then paused and offered it to the girl instead.

Aira: "Do you want to write it?"

The girl shook her head so sharply her hair struck her cheek.

Aira accepted the answer without argument. That was progress.

Pellar took the blank scrap.

His hand shook worse than Mira's had that morning.

Pellar: "What should it say?"

The girl looked at the tray again.

Girl: "Take what helps. More can come." Pellar wrote it.

His lettering was too narrow, crowded at the edges by fear of using too much paper.

Mira did not correct him.

Pellar taped the sign above the tray.

**TAKE WHAT HELPS. MORE CAN COME.**

For several minutes, no one took anything.

Then the girl took two oranges.

She held them against her sweater like stolen suns and walked back toward the planter without looking at anyone. Pellar watched her go.

Pellar: "I almost made it bad."

Iven thought about perfect copies, ugly copies, boxes, ledgers, balance columns, and all the ways rescue could become another room if people were too frightened to leave anything unmeasured.

Iven: "Almost is better than after."

Pellar looked at the torn column in his hand.

Pellar: "Can I keep this?"

Iven did not understand why anyone would want to keep a mistake. Then he did.

Iven: "Yes." He pulled his sweater closer, eyes on the floor.

Pellar folded the torn balance column and put it in his pocket with the care of someone carrying a private warning. Aira exhaled.

Aira: "I hate how educational this has become."

Mira: "You love educational things."

Aira: "I love educational things when I am the one doing the educating."

Mira smiled before she could make it polite.

Mira: "That is visible." Aira looked personally injured.

Iven took one wrapped sweet from the tray.

Then, after thinking about the sign, took a second. No one wrote it down.

The sky over Aurelis had turned violet, and the lamps along the courtyard paths lit themselves one by one. At the fountain, Halden still stood with President Valmont over the old map. Neither looked happy. That made Iven think the map was telling the truth.

The water at the fountain's center darkened briefly. Not black like Haru's Circle. Older.

Less like color than the place color had failed to arrive.

Iven felt his Green Circle warm against his wrist.

The dark reflection formed the suggestion of a ring under the academy stones, broken at four points, with a fifth space left empty at the center.

Then it vanished. No alarm sounded. No one screamed.

Halden grabbed the edge of the fountain like a man whose scholarly joy had just tried to drag him into a cellar.

President Valmont said something Iven could not hear.

Halden nodded immediately, which meant she had either threatened him or become extremely reasonable in a more dangerous tone.

Circle Zero could wait one more night.

Iven thought that was right.

Some doors should learn patience before opening.

He returned to the recovery wing with two copies in his pocket. One said:

**THIS IS NOT A TRADE.**

One said:

**THIS IS NOT A TRIAL.**

He did not know which one he needed more. So he kept both.

## Coda: The Name After the Bell

The younger transfer girl found Iven near the north planter the next morning.

She carried one orange and sat with the low wall between them. Close enough to speak. Far enough that neither body became a demand.

Iven broke his bread and left half on the stone.

She placed the orange beside it.

Girl: "Not trade."

Iven: "I know."

She studied him until she believed he might.

The cracked west bell rang late. Students crossed the courtyard without arranging themselves around the two Green Circle children.

After the last note, the girl told Iven her name. Quietly.

He repeated it once and got one sound wrong. She corrected him. He tried again.

This time she stole the smaller piece of bread. He let her.

The fountain darkened at its center before either of them finished eating. Four breaks appeared in the reflected ring below Aurelis. A fifth space remained open.

Pale writing moved beneath the water:

**THE FIFTH TOWER REMEMBERS.**

Iven did not run for Haru. He called Mira.

That difference was the first answer.

===== EPISODE 31 =====

# Episode 31: **The Fifth Tower Remembers**

The fifth tower remembered before any adult agreed it existed, which made it a problem before anyone could name one.

Adults preferred memory after classification. They liked a thing to sit quietly inside a category before it moved, glowed, accused anyone, or wrote impossible sentences under fountain water in front of students still carrying breakfast trays.

The old water did not wait.

By the time I reached the courtyard, three copies of the line already existed and none of them matched.

Mira stood at the fountain rim with ink on her fingers, two pencils behind one ear, and the expression of someone who had been asked to preserve weather. Aira crouched beside her with one knee on the stone, copying too fast and swearing too quietly for the younger students to hear. Professor Halden leaned over the fountain from the other side, hands braced on the rim, his face pale with the kind of scholarly delight that looked dangerous without supervision.

President Valmont supervised him by existing nearby. That seemed wise.

The fountain water stayed clear, which made it worse.

If the old system had blackened the basin, opened a ring, thrown silver glyphs into the air, or done any of the other dramatic things ancient magic seemed to enjoy when it wanted everyone to stop breathing properly, the academy would have known how to panic. There were procedures now. Too many, probably. Red seals, Blue stabilizers, Green evacuation routes, Yellow containment exceptions, Council witness rails, healer priority lines, Aira's growing collection of labels that made adults regret wording, cold stone and the smell of drying ink anchoring the words.

Clear water gave them nothing to fight.

Only a sentence that had appeared for one breath after the cracked west bell rang late:

**THE FIFTH TOWER REMEMBERS.**

Mira had copied it first. Her copy said:

**THE FIFTH TOWER REMAINS.**

She had crossed out the last word before the ink dried. Aira's first copy said:

**THE FIFTH WITNESS REMEMBERS.**

She had stared at it for ten full seconds, then written beside it:

**WRONG? MAYBE. DO NOT BURN.**

Halden's copy said:

**THE FIFTH TOWER REMEMBERS BELOW.**
